groups.title: French wine regions
groups.explanation: Each region gives its name to the wine made within it.

groups.title: Shades of red
groups.explanation: All four are reds, from bright scarlet to the deepest burgundy.

groups.title: French cheeses
groups.explanation: These cheeses are made in France and named after the places that make them.

sources.excerpt: Although some producers have benefited in recent years from rising prices and increased demand for prestige wines from Burgundy and Bordeaux, competition from New World wines has contributed to a decline in the domestic and international consumption of French wine to 40 liters per capita.
Champagne became associated with royalty and luxury in the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries.

Alsace is known for being the only French wine-growing region with a long practice in varietal labeling, which was a German tradition long before varietally labelled New World wines scored considerable export success.
In some vintages, Beaujolais produces more wine than the Burgundy wine regions of Chablis, Côte d'Or, Côte Chalonnaise, and Mâconnais put together.
According to surveys in Europe and the United States, scarlet and other bright shades of red are the colors most associated with courage, force, passion, heat, and joy.
The color is described as dark red, deep crimson, deeper burgundy, deep red chocolate, as dark hazelnut and velvety maroon.
It is a dark red-orange, dark vermilion, rufous color.
"Brie" is a style of cheese, and is not in itself a protected name, although some regional bries are protected.
It is similar to Camembert, which is native to a different region of France.
Roquefort is white, tangy, creamy and slightly moist, with veins of blue mold.
Comté (French pronunciation: [kɔ̃te] ), also known as Gruyère de Comté, is a hard cheese made from unpasteurised cow's milk in eastern France.
